sets.title: Ten-Room Building - Dice Numbers, Coded Letters and Seating
sets.context:
A 10-room building has floors 1-7: odd floors (1, 3, 5, 7) have one room each, even floors (2, 4, 6) have two rooms each.
Arrangement 1 (room numbers): Dice outputs in order: (6,5), (1,1), (6,3), (3,5), (2,3), (4,3), (1,4), (3,4), (4,4), (1,2). Reading left to right, first fill one room on each even floor in decreasing floor order (6, 4, 2), then fill each odd floor in increasing order (1, 3, 5, 7), then fill the remaining (second) room on each even floor in decreasing floor order (6, 4, 2) again. For an even floor's room, add the pair's two digits; for an odd floor's room, multiply them.
Arrangement 2 (letters): Letters E, V, I, F, A, H, R, M, T, P are assigned to the 10 room-numbers. The vowels (A, E, I) go to the odd prime numbers among the room-numbers, largest number first, in alphabetical order of the vowels (largest odd prime gets A, next gets E, smallest gets I). The letters before L alphabetically (F, H) go to the perfect-square numbers among the room-numbers, smallest number first, alphabetical order of the letters (smaller square gets F, larger gets H). The remaining letters (M, P, R, T, V) go to the remaining numbers, smallest number first, alphabetical order of the letters.
Arrangement 3 (seating): The 10 letters sit in a line, all facing north.
- The number of letters between I and A equals the number of persons between I and E.
- No vowel sits at either end of the line.
- The number of letters between I and E is an even prime number.
- Three persons sit between I and whoever lives on floor 1.
- M sits immediately right of V.
- R sits fourth to the left of E.
- H sits at one end of the line.
- Whoever's room is on floor 5 sits immediately right of whoever holds an even square number.

sets.title: Hexagon Triangles - Letter/Number Recoding Rules
sets.context:
At each corner of a hexagon a triangle holds a pair (either two letters or two numbers). Rules (more than one can apply to a pair):
I. If a number is a perfect square, increase only that number by 1.
II. If a letter-pair has at least one vowel, change the vowel to the preceding letter of the alphabet.
III. If both digits of a number-pair are odd, reduce each by 2.
IV. If a consonant is alphabetically smaller than N, change it to the next letter.
(If no condition applies, there is no change.)
Worked example: Triangle1 1,4 -> 2,5; Triangle2 o,k -> n,l; Triangle3 6,7 -> 6,7; Triangle4 i,l -> h,m; Triangle5 s,v -> s,v; Triangle6 5,5 -> 3,3.
Input:

Triangle2: u, b
Triangle3: 7, 7
Triangle4: h, f
Triangle5: w, q
Triangle6: 8, 3

sets.title: RC: ChatGPT in Education
sets.context:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into our daily lives. From personalized recommendations to automated customer service, AI has significantly impacted our lives. One of the latest AI technology-based platforms to disrupt the industry is ChatGPT, a Machine Learning (ML)-based system that can understand and respond to human queries.

Although ChatGPT is a promising technology in the education space, there's still a lot of R&D work to be done to integrate it into existing systems and ensure that it aligns with educational quality, policies, and standards. Furthermore, there are concerns about plagiarism, accuracy, the possibility of biases in algorithms, and security when using AI in the classroom. And even though ChatGPT can be useful for students, it's important to use it in moderation. Because, presently, ChatGPT is trained on a large amount of data, and it still depends on the accuracy of available data, which leads to limitations in its knowledge and understanding. This can lead to inaccurate or unreliable answers, especially on complex or nuanced subjects.

Additionally, a student's reliance on ChatGPT can stifle creativity and critical thinking skills. ChatGPT helps streamline routine tasks, but don't expect it to do all the heavy lifting in all areas in its present state. It might not be the best tool for the job if you're looking to dive deep into a topic or solve a complex problem. It presents a unique challenge to the current education system. The challenge for educators is to find a way to use ChatGPT without sacrificing teacher control - this is a complicated task, requiring a careful balancing act between human and machine learning. For example, a teacher understands a student's strengths and lacunae. Accordingly, by teaching/discussing, the teacher navigates the student to understand the subject. Machines are yet to learn from this kind of human touch-based teaching.

One of the primary benefits of ChatGPT is that it can significantly increase the efficiency and effectiveness of teachers in generic subjects. It can help teachers save time and energy by streamlining the teaching process by providing tailored responses to students' questions. This frees their time and energy to focus on more complex tasks, such as helping students develop problem-solving skills. To be accurate and to avoid any possible biases in the output of ChatGPT, people may expect explainability from AI models - being able to figure out why the model made the decisions and responses it did. It's important to make sure AI models are trustworthy and used ethically.

As far as sustainability is concerned, advanced AI systems like ChatGPT require vast computational power and ongoing training, which can have a pretty big energy consumption and carbon footprint. While ChatGPT is a cool technology with a lot of potential benefits, we need to keep sustainability and explainability in mind as we move forward with it. We need to find ways to minimize the environmental impact as well as train young human brains to develop their logic and analytical skills by being less dependent on the machine and using AI in a responsible and sustainable way.

sets.title: RC: Urban Agriculture and Food Security
sets.context:
[Passage paraphrased from the original]
Urban agriculture describes farming practices carried out within urban and peri-urban areas - peri-urban zones being the transition space between purely rural land use (farming, livestock) and purely urban land use (built environment, manufacturing, services), sitting between the outer edge of urban/regional centres and the countryside proper. Urban agriculture spans a wide range of food and non-food output, including livestock rearing, aquaculture, beekeeping, and commercial-scale floriculture.

However, despite this variety, urban agriculture is improbable to include the cultivation of staple foods, given the complexity involved (soil management, irrigation, transplantation, mechanisation, harvesting) and the large land area such crops demand. What urban agriculture will predominantly grow instead are foods that supply micronutrients - fruits, vegetables, dark leafy greens, fish, and legumes - compounds needed only in small quantities but essential to the body's growth, development, and maintenance.

Urban agriculture covers livelihood systems ranging from subsistence production at the household level up to fully commercialised agriculture; this adaptability to diverse urban situations and stakeholders is one of its defining attributes. It is increasingly being adopted worldwide by urban local bodies (ULBs), entrepreneurs, non-governmental organisations, community groups, and individual citizens. The United Nations' Food and Agricultural Organization considers urban and peri-urban agriculture important to global food and nutritional security, and promotes such activity through its Urban Food Agenda.

The Urban Food Agenda comprises policies, programmes, and initiatives developed with civil society, academia, international agencies, city entities, and the private sector. In recent years, urban and peri-urban areas worldwide are estimated to have produced 5-10 percent of the world's legumes, vegetables and tubers, and 15-20 percent of all food. The world is becoming steadily more urban - 68 percent of the global population, projected to rise to 9.8 billion by 2050, is expected to live in cities by then, meaning cities will also consume the bulk (80 percent) of all food produced globally.

Importantly, by 2050 the arable land available per person will have shrunk to one-third of its 1970 level, due to climate change, declining fisheries, and degradation from overfarming and poor production practices. Given this, the social, economic, and environmental sustainability of food systems and evolution of urban diets will largely depend on managing food systems in urban and peri-urban areas - making a stronger focus on the Urban Food Agenda long overdue, so ULBs and other relevant stakeholders can plan urban areas adequately.

questions.question:
Direction: Some symbols are used with the meanings given below. Coded statements are given followed by three conclusions. Take the statements as true even if they seem to be at variance from commonly known facts.
P @ Q means Only a few Q are P.
P # Q means All Q are P.
P $ Q means No Q is P.
Statement:
K @ J # C $ D; K # B
Conclusions:
I. All D is J is a possibility.
II. No J is K.
III. Some D is not K.
questions.explanation: Decoding: K@J = only a few J are K (some J are K, some are not); J#C = all C are J; C$D = no D is C; K#B = all B are K. Since C is a subset of J but D is entirely outside C, D could still lie entirely within the rest of J, so 'All D is J' remains a live possibility - conclusion I holds. 'Only a few J are K' already guarantees some J-K overlap exists, directly contradicting 'No J is K' - so II is false. Nothing links D to K at all (D only relates to C), so it is not fixed that some D is not K (D could conceivably lie wholly within K) - III does not definitely follow. Hence only I follows.

source.ref: SBI PO Mains 2023 (memory-based, Testbook Mains book)

Equation (i): the n-th root of (qn), multiplied by (p+1), equals 27, where 'p' is the largest even prime number.
Equation (ii): (q + m - n)^2 = 64.
Find the sum of q, m, and n.
(I): (x-1) and (x+1) are factors of the equation mx^3 + nx^2 - 2x - 3 = 0.
(II): q = n+6 and 2m+q = 13.
options: The data in statement I alone is sufficient, while the data in statement II alone is not sufficient
The data in statement II alone is sufficient, while the data in statement I alone is not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone is sufficient
The data in both statements I and II together are necessary
The data given in both statements I and II together are not sufficient
questions.explanation: With p=2 (largest even prime), equation (i) becomes the n-th root of (qn) x 3 = 27. Statement I: plugging x=1 and x=-1 into mx^3+nx^2-2x-3=0 (since (x-1),(x+1) are factors) gives m+n=5 and n-m=1, so n=3, m=2; combined with equation (ii), (q+2-3)^2=64 gives q=9 or q=-7, and equation (i) selects the valid q=9, so q+m+n=14 is pinned. Statement II gives q=n+6 and 2m+q=13, which combined with equation (ii) and equation (i) converges on the same m=2, n=3, q=9 (the other algebraic branch being ruled out by equation (i)). Either statement alone, together with the two given equations, therefore fixes the sum.

questions.question:
Yash invests Rs. X in scheme 'A' at the rate of R% compounded annually for t years. Find the value of X.
(I): Kush invests (X+1000) Rs. for (t+2) years in the same scheme at the rate of R% compounded annually and gets 44% more amount than Yash.
(II): If Piyush invests the same amount as Yash for 2 years in the same scheme at the same rate of compound interest, he gets Rs. 3456 as the total amount.
options: The data in statement I alone is sufficient, while statement II alone is not sufficient
The data in statement II alone is sufficient, while statement I alone is not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone is sufficient
The data in both statements I and II together are necessary
The data given in both statements I and II together are not sufficient
questions.explanation: Statement I alone relates X, R and t through a single equation with three unknowns - not enough on its own. Statement II alone gives X(1+R/100)^2=3456, one equation in X and R - also not enough alone. Combining them, the '(t+2)' term in statement I's equation cancels against the '(1+R/100)^t' factor, leaving (X+1000)(1+R/100)^2 = 1.44X; substituting (1+R/100)^2=3456/X from statement II turns this into a single equation purely in X, which can then be solved - so both statements together are necessary.

questions.question:
The ratio of time taken by pipe 'A' and pipe 'B' to fill the same tank is 3:4. Pipe 'A' takes t hours to fill the tank, and pipe 'C' takes (t+4) hours to completely empty the same tank. If all three pipes are opened together at 10 am, the tank gets filled at 5 pm. For how many hours was pipe C opened during the process, given that pipe 'C' was closed at some point in between?
(I): Pipe 'A' and pipe 'C' together can fill (7/10)th of the tank in 28 hours.
(II): Pipe 'A' and pipe 'B' together can fill (7/8)th of the tank in 3 hours.
options: The data in statement I alone is sufficient, while statement II alone is not sufficient
The data in statement II alone is sufficient, while statement I alone is not sufficient
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone is sufficient
The data given in both statements I and II together are not sufficient
The data in both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: Statement II alone pins down t directly: (1/t + 3/(4t)) x 3 = 7/8 gives t=6 hours, and with the tank filling in the fixed 7-hour (10am-5pm) window, the time pipe C was open can then be worked out from pipe C's known (t+4)=10-hour emptying time. Statement I alone similarly gives an equation in t from pipe A and C's combined rate over 28 hours, which (together with the fixed 7-hour window and t+4 emptying time) is likewise enough to pin down how long C was open. So either statement alone suffices.

A. There are several concerns associated with using AI in the classroom such as big energy consumption and carbon footprint.
B. People may expect explainability from AI models, which means being able to figure out why the model made the decisions and responses it did.
C. The ChatGPT model significantly increases the efficiency and effectiveness of teachers in generic subjects and frees their time and energy to focus on more complex tasks, such as helping students develop problem-solving skills.
questions.explanation: The passage lists plagiarism, accuracy, algorithmic bias and security as classroom-specific AI concerns - energy consumption and carbon footprint are raised separately, under sustainability, not as a classroom concern - so A misattributes and cannot be inferred. B and C both restate passage content accurately, so they can be inferred; only A cannot.

B. The world is increasingly becoming more urban, with 68 percent of the global population - estimated to drop to 9.8 billion by 2050 - expected to reside in urban areas by that year.
C. As per the United Nations' Food and Agricultural Organization, urban and peri-urban agriculture have an important role in global food and nutritional security, and thus it is aiming to encourage such activities through the Urban Food Agenda.
